units.title: The Real Numbers
units.blurb: Absolute value and the triangle inequality, suprema and infima, completeness, the density of the rationals, and the sizes of infinite sets.

units.title: Sequences and Their Limits
units.blurb: The ε–N definition and proofs that use it, bounded and monotone sequences, subsequences, lim sup and lim inf, and Cauchy sequences.

units.title: Series
units.blurb: Convergence as a statement about partial sums: the Cauchy criterion, comparison, condensation, the root test with lim sup, alternating series and rearrangements.

units.title: Limits of Functions and Continuity
units.blurb: Limits and continuity with ε and δ, the sequential criterion, the intermediate and extreme value theorems, and uniform continuity.

units.title: Derivatives
units.blurb: Derivatives from the definition, differentiability, the mean value theorem and the bounds it gives, and Taylor's theorem with remainder.

units.title: The Riemann Integral
units.blurb: Upper and lower sums, the integrability criterion, which functions are integrable, bounds for integrals, and a proof of the fundamental theorem.

units.title: Sequences and Series of Functions
units.blurb: Pointwise and uniform convergence, the sup norm, what uniform limits keep, the Weierstrass M-test and power series.

units.title: Metric Spaces
units.blurb: Distance in general: metrics, open and closed sets, compact sets and the contraction mapping theorem.

topics.title: Absolute Value and the Triangle Inequality
topics.short: |x − a| < ε means x is within ε of a; |a + b| ≤ |a| + |b| and |a| − |b| ≤ |a − b| turn distances into bounds.
topics.trouble: Students write |a − b| ≤ |a| − |b| (backward) or treat |a + b| = |a| + |b| as always true. The reverse triangle inequality gives a lower bound: |a − b| ≥ |a| − |b|.

topics.title: Supremum and Infimum
topics.short: The supremum of a set is its least upper bound and the infimum its greatest lower bound; neither has to belong to the set.
topics.trouble: Students confuse sup with max and think the sup must be an element of the set, or give an upper bound that is not the least one.

topics.title: The ε-Test for a Supremum
topics.short: An upper bound s is the supremum exactly when, for every ε > 0, some element of the set is bigger than s − ε.
topics.trouble: Students show that s is an upper bound and stop. That proves sup A ≤ s; the ε-test is what shows no smaller number is an upper bound.

topics.title: Completeness and the Archimedean Property
topics.short: Every nonempty set of reals that is bounded above has a supremum; from it, for every ε > 0 some whole number n has 1/n < ε.
topics.trouble: Students assume a bounded set of rationals has a rational supremum. The rationals with x² < 2 are bounded, but their supremum √2 is not rational.

topics.title: Density of the Rationals
topics.short: Between any two real numbers a < b lies a rational: pick n with 1/n < b − a, and some multiple m/n lands strictly between them.
topics.trouble: Students pick n with 1/n ≤ b − a, which can land exactly on b, or forget to check that m/n is strictly bigger than a.

topics.title: Countable and Uncountable Sets
topics.short: A set is countable when its elements can be listed a₁, a₂, a₃, …; the rationals are countable, but Cantor's diagonal argument shows the reals are not.
topics.trouble: Students think the diagonal number might appear later in the list. It differs from the nth number in the nth digit, so it differs from every number on the list.

topics.title: The Definition of a Limit (ε–N)
topics.short: aₙ → L when for every ε > 0 there is an N with |aₙ − L| < ε for all n ≥ N; for a given ε you can find such an N and check it.
topics.trouble: Students check a single term instead of every term from N on, or think there is only one right N. Any larger N works too.

topics.title: Writing ε–N Proofs
topics.short: Work backward on scratch paper to find N in terms of ε; then write the proof forward: let ε > 0, choose N, take n ≥ N and show |aₙ − L| < ε.
topics.trouble: Students hand in the scratch work, which starts from the inequality they want to prove, or choose an N that depends on n.

topics.title: Bounded Sequences and Divergence
topics.short: Every convergent sequence is bounded; to show aₙ does not converge to L, find one ε > 0 for which no N works.
topics.trouble: Students think a bounded sequence must converge ((−1)ⁿ does not), or negate the definition as "for every ε no N works" instead of "some ε has no N that works."

topics.title: Proving the Limit Laws
topics.short: If aₙ → a and bₙ → b, then aₙ + bₙ → a + b and aₙbₙ → ab; the proofs split ε between the two pieces and use that convergent sequences are bounded.
topics.trouble: Students use one N for both sequences without taking N = max(N₁, N₂), or forget to bound |aₙ| in the product proof.

topics.title: Order Limits and the Squeeze Theorem
topics.short: Limits keep ≤: if aₙ ≤ bₙ then lim aₙ ≤ lim bₙ; and a sequence trapped between two sequences with the same limit has that limit too.
topics.trouble: Students conclude lim aₙ < lim bₙ from aₙ < bₙ. Strict inequalities can become equal in the limit: 0 < 1/n, but both sides tend to 0.

topics.title: The Monotone Convergence Theorem
topics.short: A bounded monotone sequence converges, to the supremum of its terms if it increases; for aₙ₊₁ = g(aₙ), show monotone and bounded, then solve L = g(L).
topics.trouble: Students solve L = g(L) before showing that a limit exists, or keep the wrong root of the fixed-point equation.

topics.title: Subsequences and Subsequential Limits
topics.short: Every subsequence of a convergent sequence has the same limit, so two subsequences with different limits prove that a sequence diverges.
topics.trouble: Students treat any reordering of the terms as a subsequence. The indices must strictly increase: a₂, a₄, a₆, … is a subsequence; a₄, a₂, a₆, … is not.

topics.title: The Bolzano–Weierstrass Theorem
topics.short: Every bounded sequence has a convergent subsequence: halve the interval again and again, each time keeping a half that holds infinitely many terms.
topics.trouble: Students keep the half that holds more of the first few terms, instead of a half that holds infinitely many; or think the theorem says the whole sequence converges.

topics.title: Limit Superior and Limit Inferior
topics.short: lim sup aₙ is the limit of the tail suprema sup{aₖ : k ≥ n}; it is the largest subsequential limit, and aₙ converges exactly when lim sup aₙ = lim inf aₙ.
topics.trouble: Students give the largest term of the sequence (its supremum) instead of the limit of the tail suprema; the two differ whenever a big early term is never matched again.

topics.title: Cauchy Sequences
topics.short: aₙ is Cauchy when for every ε > 0 some N makes |aₘ − aₙ| < ε for all m, n ≥ N; in ℝ a sequence is Cauchy exactly when it converges.
topics.trouble: Students check only consecutive terms. |aₙ₊₁ − aₙ| → 0 is not enough: the partial sums of 1/n creep apart forever.

topics.title: Series and the Cauchy Criterion
topics.short: ∑aₖ converges when its partial sums do; by the Cauchy criterion, blocks aₘ₊₁ + ⋯ + aₙ far out must be small, and in particular aₖ → 0.
topics.trouble: Students think aₖ → 0 is enough. The harmonic series has terms that go to 0, but every block 1/(n + 1) + ⋯ + 1/(2n) is at least 1/2.

topics.title: Comparison and Absolute Convergence
topics.short: If |aₖ| ≤ bₖ and ∑bₖ converges, the Cauchy criterion makes ∑aₖ converge; in particular, absolute convergence implies convergence.
topics.trouble: Students run the comparison the wrong way: being smaller than a divergent series, or bigger than a convergent one, proves nothing.

topics.title: The Cauchy Condensation Test
topics.short: For a decreasing sequence of positive terms, ∑aₙ and ∑2ᵏa₂ₖ converge or diverge together; it settles the p-series and ∑1/(n(ln n)ᵖ).
topics.trouble: Students forget the factor 2ᵏ, or apply the test to terms that are not decreasing.

topics.title: Root and Ratio Tests with lim sup
topics.short: If lim sup |aₖ|^(1/k) < 1 the series converges absolutely, and if it is > 1 the series diverges; the root test works even when the ratios jump around.
topics.trouble: Students use lim and get stuck when the ratios or roots don't settle down, or read a lim sup of 1 as divergence. A value of 1 decides nothing.

topics.title: Alternating Series and Error Bounds
topics.short: If bₖ decreases to 0, ∑(−1)ᵏ⁺¹bₖ converges, and the error after n terms is less than bₙ₊₁: the partial sums zigzag and trap the sum.
topics.trouble: Students use bₙ instead of bₙ₊₁ for the error, or skip checking that bₖ decreases.

topics.title: Rearranging Series
topics.short: Rearranging an absolutely convergent series keeps its sum; a conditionally convergent series can be rearranged to add up to any number you like (Riemann).
topics.trouble: Students assume that the order of the terms never matters. For infinitely many terms it does, unless the series converges absolutely.

topics.title: Limits of Functions (ε–δ)
topics.short: lim f(x) = L as x → a when for every ε > 0 some δ > 0 gives |f(x) − L| < ε whenever 0 < |x − a| < δ; any smaller positive δ works too.
topics.trouble: Students think there is one right δ, or let δ depend on x. Any positive δ up to the largest one that works is a correct answer.

topics.title: Continuity with ε and δ
topics.short: f is continuous at a when for every ε > 0 some δ > 0 gives |f(x) − f(a)| < ε whenever |x − a| < δ; for x² the classic choice is δ = min(1, ε/(2|a| + 1)).
topics.trouble: Students bound |x + a| without first restricting x (the "min with 1" step), or end with a δ that depends on x.

topics.title: The Sequential Criterion and Discontinuity
topics.short: f is continuous at a exactly when f(xₙ) → f(a) for every sequence xₙ → a; two sequences giving different limits prove a discontinuity.
topics.trouble: Students test one sequence and conclude that f is continuous. One sequence can prove a discontinuity, but continuity needs every sequence.

topics.title: The Intermediate Value Theorem
topics.short: A continuous function on [a, b] takes every value between f(a) and f(b); the proof uses c = sup{x : f(x) < 0}, and bisection traps c to any accuracy.
topics.trouble: Students apply the theorem to a function that is not continuous on the whole closed interval, like 1/x on [−1, 1], or think it tells where the root is.

topics.title: The Extreme Value Theorem
topics.short: A continuous function on a closed, bounded interval attains a maximum and a minimum; drop any hypothesis and the supremum may not be attained.
topics.trouble: Students use it on open or unbounded intervals. On (0, 1), f(x) = x has supremum 1 but no maximum.

topics.title: Uniform Continuity
topics.short: f is uniformly continuous on S when one δ works for every point of S at once; continuous functions on [a, b] are, but 1/x on (0, 1) is not.
topics.trouble: Students find a δ that depends on the point and call it uniform. If the best δ shrinks to 0 as the point moves, no single δ works.

topics.title: Derivatives from the Definition
topics.short: f′(a) = lim (f(a + h) − f(a))/h as h → 0; the definition handles what the rules can't, like x² sin(1/x) at 0.
topics.trouble: Students apply the rules to a piecewise formula at the break point instead of going back to the definition there.

topics.title: Differentiability and Continuity
topics.short: Differentiable at a implies continuous at a, but not conversely; at a break point the one-sided derivatives must exist and agree.
topics.trouble: Students check that the pieces meet and forget to match the slopes, or match the slopes and forget that the pieces must meet.

topics.title: Rolle's Theorem and the Mean Value Theorem
topics.short: If f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b), some c in (a, b) has f′(c) = (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a); Rolle's theorem is the case f(a) = f(b).
topics.trouble: Students skip the hypotheses (|x| on [−1, 1] has no such c) or report a c outside (a, b).

topics.title: Inequalities from the Mean Value Theorem
topics.short: If |f′| ≤ K on an interval, then |f(x) − f(y)| ≤ K|x − y| there; this proves bounds like |sin x − sin y| ≤ |x − y| and gives δ = ε/K.
topics.trouble: Students use the value of f′ at one point instead of a bound for |f′| over the whole interval.

topics.title: Taylor's Theorem with Remainder
topics.short: f(x) = Pₙ(x) + f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(c)(x − a)ⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1)! for some c between a and x; a bound on f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾ bounds the error.
topics.trouble: Students use the nth derivative instead of the (n + 1)st, or plug in a guess for c instead of bounding the derivative over the whole interval.

topics.title: Upper and Lower Sums
topics.short: For a partition P, U(f, P) uses the supremum of f on each piece and L(f, P) the infimum; every lower sum is at most every upper sum, and refining P brings them together.
topics.trouble: Students use left and right endpoints for a function that is not monotone; the sup or inf on a piece can sit inside it, at a turning point.

topics.title: The Integrability Criterion
topics.short: f is integrable exactly when for every ε > 0 some partition has U(f, P) − L(f, P) < ε; for monotone f on n equal pieces the gap is |f(b) − f(a)|(b − a)/n.
topics.trouble: Students show that U − L is small for one partition and stop. The criterion needs a partition for every ε > 0.

topics.title: Which Functions Are Integrable
topics.short: Continuous functions, monotone functions and bounded functions with finitely many jumps are integrable; Dirichlet's function is not, since every U = b − a and every L = 0.
topics.trouble: Students think every bounded function is integrable, or that a function with a jump cannot be.

topics.title: Bounds and the Mean Value Theorem for Integrals
topics.short: If m ≤ f ≤ M on [a, b], then m(b − a) ≤ ∫f ≤ M(b − a); a continuous f equals its average value at some c in [a, b].
topics.trouble: Students bound the integral with values of f at the endpoints instead of its true minimum and maximum on the interval.

topics.title: Proving the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
topics.short: F(x) = ∫ₐˣ f is continuous, and F′(c) = f(c) wherever f is continuous; at a jump of f, F has a corner.
topics.trouble: Students assume F′ = f everywhere, even at a jump of f, where F has different one-sided derivatives.

topics.title: Limits of Sums as Integrals
topics.short: Because continuous functions are integrable, every Riemann sum tends to the integral; so a limit like (1/n)∑f(k/n) is ∫₀¹ f(x) dx.
topics.trouble: Students match the sum to the wrong interval, or lose the factor 1/n that plays the role of Δx.

topics.title: Pointwise Convergence
topics.short: fₙ → f pointwise when fₙ(x) → f(x) at each x separately; a pointwise limit of continuous functions can jump, as xⁿ on [0, 1] does.
topics.trouble: Students find the limit for most x and miss the special points, such as x = 1 for xⁿ, where the limit is different.

topics.title: Uniform Convergence and the Sup Norm
topics.short: fₙ → f uniformly when ‖fₙ − f‖ = sup |fₙ(x) − f(x)| → 0: one N works for every x at once.
topics.trouble: Students fix x, watch |fₙ(x) − f(x)| go to 0, and call it uniform. That is pointwise; the supremum over all x is what must go to 0.

topics.title: What Uniform Convergence Keeps
topics.short: A uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous, and ∫fₙ → ∫f; without uniform convergence, the limit of the integrals can differ from the integral of the limit.
topics.trouble: Students swap a limit with an integral or a derivative without checking uniform convergence.

topics.title: The Weierstrass M-Test
topics.short: If |fₖ(x)| ≤ Mₖ for every x and ∑Mₖ converges, then ∑fₖ converges uniformly (and absolutely).
topics.trouble: Students choose an Mₖ that depends on x, or a bound whose series diverges.

topics.title: Power Series: Radius and Uniform Convergence
topics.short: ∑cₙxⁿ has radius R = 1/lim sup |cₙ|^(1/n); it converges uniformly on every [−r, r] with r < R, so its sum is continuous inside the interval.
topics.trouble: Students use the ratio test on a series with gaps (only even powers, say), where the ratios don't have a limit; the lim sup of the nth roots handles it.

topics.title: Metric Spaces
topics.short: A metric d measures distance: d(x, y) > 0 unless x = y, d(x, y) = d(y, x), and d(x, z) ≤ d(x, y) + d(y, z); the taxicab, Euclidean and max metrics on ℝ² are three examples.
topics.trouble: Students check positivity and symmetry but skip the triangle inequality; d(x, y) = (x − y)² passes the first two and fails the third.

topics.title: Open and Closed Sets
topics.short: A set is open when every point has a ball around it inside the set, and closed when it contains all its limit points; the closure adds the limit points.
topics.trouble: Students think "not open" means closed. [0, 1) is neither open nor closed, and ℝ is both.

topics.title: Compact Sets
topics.short: K is compact when every open cover has a finite subcover; in ℝⁿ that happens exactly when K is closed and bounded (Heine–Borel).
topics.trouble: Students show that one cover has a finite subcover and stop; compactness is about every open cover. Others call (0, 1] compact because it is bounded.

topics.title: The Contraction Mapping Theorem
topics.short: If d(g(x), g(y)) ≤ k·d(x, y) with k < 1 on a complete space, g has exactly one fixed point, and the nth iterate is within kⁿd(x₁, x₀)/(1 − k) of it.
topics.trouble: Students check |g′| < 1 at one point instead of on the whole set, or forget that g must map the set into itself.
